in_scope_clauses.summary:
Quality management system and its processes — IATF 16949 extends
ISO 9001 §4.4 with automotive-specific process effectiveness and
efficiency criteria, plus product-safety process discipline.

Calibration / verification records — automotive-specific
retention discipline for measurement traceability across
production tooling and inspection equipment. Equivalent to
AS9100D §7.1.5 and ISO 13485 §7.6 in adjacent verticals.

Documented information — creation, control, distribution,
access, retrieval, storage, preservation, retention, and
disposition of documented information required by the QMS,
including customer-specific requirements (CSRs).

Special characteristics — identification, documentation, and
flow-down of customer-designated and supplier-identified
special characteristics (Key Characteristics, Critical
Characteristics, Safety Characteristics) through PFMEA, Control
Plan, and PPAP. Drives variation-control discipline at all
stages of production.

Control of externally-provided processes, products and services
(supplier controls). Selection, evaluation, monitoring;
flow-down of customer-specific requirements; sub-supplier
monitoring (Tier-N visibility); supplier QMS development to
IATF 16949 or ISO 9001 with automotive-customer-specific
additions.

Control plan — documented per-part / per-product-family plan
describing controls (process parameters, characteristics,
measurement methods, sampling frequencies, reaction plans) at
each step from receiving through shipping. Living document
updated whenever the process or product changes. Bridges
PFMEA + work instructions + inspection.

Control of nonconforming outputs — segregation, identification,
disposition (rework / regrade / use-as-is via deviation
authorization / scrap), and concession-from-customer handling
where applicable. Includes customer-notification protocol for
shipped nonconforming product.

Internal audit — including the IATF-mandated three audit types:
QMS audit (full-scope), manufacturing process audit (per process
at planned intervals), and product audit (per product family
including layout inspection). Auditor competence requirements
per §7.2.3.

Problem solving — automotive 8D-style structured approach
(Define, Form Team, Describe, Containment, Root Cause,
Permanent Corrective Action, Verify Implementation, Prevent
Recurrence, Recognize Team). Mandatory for customer-issued
problem reports and recurring internal nonconformances.

Management of functional safety — overall safety management
(safety culture, FuSa management at organizational and project
levels, safety lifecycle planning, safety case structure).
Includes the Safety Plan, the Safety Case, and FuSa management
role definitions.

Confirmation measures — confirmation review (concept + system
design phases), functional safety audit (process compliance),
and functional safety assessment (final independent assessment
before release). Independence requirements scale with ASIL
assignment (A → B → C → D require increasingly-independent
reviewers).

Item definition — first concept-phase deliverable defining the
boundary of the "item" subject to FuSa analysis: functional
and non-functional requirements, preliminary architecture,
external interfaces, environmental conditions, legal
requirements, and dependencies on other items.

Hazard Analysis and Risk Assessment (HARA) — systematic
identification of hazardous events from item malfunctions,
classification of risk per Severity (S0-S3) × Exposure (E0-E4)
× Controllability (C0-C3), and assignment of Automotive Safety
Integrity Level (ASIL A / B / C / D / QM) per the ASIL table.
Output: Safety Goals at the item level.

Functional Safety Concept (FSC) — derivation of Functional
Safety Requirements (FSRs) from Safety Goals, allocation to
preliminary architecture, and definition of safe states +
warning + degradation strategies + fault tolerance / fault
reaction times.

Product development at the hardware level — Hardware Safety
Requirements; hardware architectural design; hardware safety
analyses; hardware metrics (Single-Point Fault Metric SPFM,
Latent Fault Metric LFM, Probabilistic Metric for Hardware
Failures PMHF) per ASIL target; hardware V&V.

Product development at the software level — Software Safety
Requirements; software architectural design with method
requirements per ASIL (e.g., MISRA C, defensive programming,
strong typing); unit / integration / qualification testing
with structural coverage requirements per ASIL (statement,
branch, MC/DC).

Supporting processes — interfaces with distributed development
(§5); requirements management (§6); configuration management
(§7); change management (§8); verification (§9); documentation
(§10); software tool qualification (§11 — tools used in safety
lifecycle must be confidence-classified TCL1 / TCL2 / TCL3 and
qualified accordingly).

ASIL-oriented and safety-oriented analyses — ASIL decomposition
(rule-bound reduction of ASIL requirements onto multiple
sufficiently-independent elements); analysis of dependent
failures (DFA — common cause + cascading failure); safety
analyses methodology (FMEA, FTA, FMEDA, ETA).

Cybersecurity Management System (CSMS) — overall organizational
cyber capability covering cybersecurity governance, cyber
culture, risk management framework, tool management, supplier
cybersecurity management, audit + assessment. Required as
precondition for project-specific cybersecurity engineering;
type-approval gate under UN R155.

Project-dependent cybersecurity management — Cybersecurity
Plan, Cybersecurity Case (analogous to FuSa Safety Case),
project-level cybersecurity activities, tailoring per the
item / component scope.

Continuous cybersecurity activities — post-development phase
including vulnerability management (monitoring, triage,
response), incident response, sustained cybersecurity (over
the entire product lifecycle including end-of-support
transitions).

Threat Analysis and Risk Assessment (TARA) — systematic
identification of damage scenarios, threat scenarios, attack
paths (using STRIDE, attack trees, or similar); rating of
impact (Safety / Financial / Operational / Privacy) and
attack feasibility; risk determination; Cybersecurity Assurance
Level (CAL) assignment; risk treatment decision. Cyber analog
of HARA.

Concept phase + product development phases — cybersecurity
goals, cybersecurity controls, cybersecurity requirements
allocated across architecture, integration + verification +
validation activities.

Manufacturer Cybersecurity Management System certification —
type-approval gate. Manufacturer must demonstrate a documented
CSMS covering organizational governance, risk management,
monitoring of cyber threats, supplier dependencies, incident
response, and processes for cybersecurity throughout the
development, production, and post-production phases.
Certificate issued by approval authority; required prior to
vehicle-type approval.

Vehicle-type cybersecurity approval — per-vehicle-type
cybersecurity assessment demonstrating manufacturer has
addressed the threats enumerated in Annex 5 (covering external
interfaces, vehicle communication channels, update process,
back-end-server interactions, vehicle data, code, user
identity, etc.) through analysis + risk treatment per the
certified CSMS.

Manufacturer Software Update Management System (SUMS)
certification — process discipline for over-the-air and
offline software updates: identification of vehicles affected
by each update, integrity of updates (signing + verification),
compatibility analysis (no breaking changes to type approval),
user information requirements, rollback capability, update
audit trail.

Software Engineering process group (SWE.1 software requirements
analysis, SWE.2 software architectural design, SWE.3 software
detailed design + unit construction, SWE.4 software unit
verification, SWE.5 software integration + integration
verification, SWE.6 software qualification test). Bidirectional
traceability between SYS / SWE / qualification levels;
capability level rating per VDA QMC scope (typically Level 2
or 3 for production software).

Management process group (MAN.3 project management, MAN.5 risk
management, MAN.6 measurement) and Support process group
(SUP.1 quality assurance, SUP.8 configuration management,
SUP.9 problem resolution management, SUP.10 change request
management). Crosscuts every SWE activity and ties to ISO 26262
Part 8 supporting processes.

Production Part Approval Process (PPAP) — the production-readiness
gate for the automotive industry, analogous to aerospace AS9102
FAI. 18-element submission package: design records, engineering
change documents, customer engineering approval, DFMEA, process
flow, PFMEA, control plan, MSA studies, dimensional results,
material/performance test results, initial process studies,
qualified laboratory documentation, appearance approval, sample
production parts, master sample, checking aids, customer-specific
requirements, Part Submission Warrant (PSW). Submission Level
1-5 determined by customer.

Govern function — cultivate and implement a culture of risk
management throughout the organization. Subcategories include
policies and procedures for AI risk management, roles and
responsibilities, accountability structures, diversity and
equity considerations, third-party AI components governance.

Map function — establish the context within which AI risks are
framed. Categorize the AI system, identify intended purposes
and use cases, identify stakeholders, characterize positive
and negative impacts to individuals and society.

Measure function — employ quantitative, qualitative, and mixed-
method tools to assess identified AI risks. Includes test sets,
benchmarks, evaluation methodologies, ongoing monitoring,
tracking of trustworthy characteristics (validity, reliability,
safety, security, accountability, transparency, explainability,
privacy, fairness).

Manage function — prioritize and respond to risks based on the
Measure outputs. Allocate resources to risks based on assessed
impact and likelihood, plan responses, monitor risks over time,
communicate to stakeholders, sunset or decommission as needed.

Risk management system for high-risk AI systems — established,
implemented, documented, and maintained throughout the AI
system lifecycle. Iterative process: identification of known
and reasonably foreseeable risks; estimation and evaluation;
adoption of risk management measures; residual risk evaluation
against acceptability criteria.

Data and data governance for high-risk AI — training,
validation, and testing datasets shall be subject to data
governance and management practices appropriate to the intended
purpose. Datasets shall be relevant, representative, free of
errors, complete; statistical properties documented; bias
examined and mitigated.

Technical documentation for high-risk AI — drawn up before
placing on the market or putting into service, kept up to date.
Demonstrates compliance with Section 2 requirements; provides
authorities with the necessary information to assess
compliance. Content per Annex IV.

Record-keeping / automatic logging — high-risk AI systems shall
automatically record events ("logs") over their lifetime to
ensure traceability appropriate to the intended purpose. Logs
enable identification of situations resulting in risk,
facilitate post-market monitoring, and support reproducibility.

Transparency and provision of information to deployers —
high-risk AI systems shall be designed and developed so their
operation is sufficiently transparent to enable deployers to
interpret outputs and use them appropriately. Accompanied by
instructions for use containing concise, complete, correct,
clear, relevant, accessible information.

Human oversight for high-risk AI — designed and developed so
they can be effectively overseen by natural persons during
use. Oversight measures must enable the natural person to fully
understand system capacities and limitations, remain aware of
automation bias, correctly interpret output, decide not to
use the system, intervene or interrupt operation.

Accuracy, robustness, and cybersecurity for high-risk AI —
designed to achieve appropriate level of accuracy, robustness,
and cybersecurity, performing consistently throughout lifecycle.
Resilience against errors, faults, inconsistencies; resilience
against unauthorized attempts to alter use, behavior, or
performance.

Artificial Intelligence Management System (AIMS) — establishment,
implementation, maintenance, and continual improvement of an
AI management system. Parallel structure to ISO 9001 / 13485:
context (§4), leadership (§5), planning (§6), support (§7),
operation (§8), performance evaluation (§9), improvement (§10).
Composes with sector-specific QMS standards as the AI-management
overlay.

Policies for information security — defined, approved by management,
published, communicated to and acknowledged by relevant personnel
and interested parties, and reviewed at planned intervals or when
significant changes occur.

Legal, statutory, regulatory, and contractual requirements relevant
to information security shall be identified, documented, and kept
up to date. The organization's approach to meeting each shall be
defined.

Separation of development, test, and production environments —
including separation of duties where appropriate — to reduce the
risk of unauthorized access or unauthorized changes to the
operational environment.

artifacts.name: Quality policy (IATF 16949 + ISO 9001:2015 binding)
Standard operating procedure (IATF 16949 calibration + special characteristics + nonconforming output)
Internal audit procedure (IATF 16949 §9.2 three-audit-type discipline)
Management review (IATF 16949 §9.3 / automotive inputs)
Approved Supplier List (IATF 16949 §8.4 external provider control with Tier-N visibility)
Supplier evaluation (IATF 16949 §8.4 with customer-specific flow-down)
CAPA issue template — 8D problem-solving entry (IATF 16949 §10.2.3)
Nonconformance report (IATF 16949 §8.7)
Functional Safety management file (ISO 26262 Part 2 — Safety Plan, Safety Case, FuSa roles)
Item Definition (ISO 26262 Part 3 §5)
Hazard Analysis and Risk Assessment (ISO 26262 Part 3 §6; ASIL derivation)
Functional Safety Concept + Technical Safety Concept (ISO 26262 Part 3 §7 + Part 4)
Verification protocol (ISO 26262 Part 5 hardware V&V)
Software test protocol (ISO 26262 Part 6 software V&V per ASIL + ASPICE SWE.4-6)
Threat Analysis and Risk Assessment (ISO/SAE 21434 §15; CAL derivation)
PPAP 18-element submission package (AIAG PPAP 4th Ed.)
AI System Card / Model Card template
AI Impact Assessment template (EU AI Act + NIST AI RMF aligned)
Software architecture (AI accuracy / robustness / cybersecurity per EU AI Act Art 15)
Technical file index (AI automatic logging per EU AI Act Art 12)
Software release record template (information-security overlay binding)
